name: Rib cartilage graft rhinoplasty

card.summary: Uses the patient's own rib cartilage for big structural rebuilds of the nose; supported by surgical case series.
card.note: Requires a second surgical site on the chest; donor site morbidity is assessed in studies.

quick.overview:
Rib cartilage rhinoplasty uses cartilage taken from the patient's rib to build or support the nose when the septum cannot supply enough. It is commonly discussed for major dorsal work and revisions.

Evidence comes from retrospective series, including a 58-patient cohort reporting stable results.
quick.mechanism: Cartilage is harvested from the rib, carved into grafts such as dorsal onlays or columellar struts, and placed in the nose.
quick.risks: The procedure adds a chest donor site, and studies track donor site morbidity, graft warping and revision need. Details beyond the cited cohort were not reviewed.

lead: Rib (costal) cartilage graft rhinoplasty is a form of nose surgery in which cartilage harvested from the patient's own rib is carved into grafts that support or build up the nose. It is used when a large amount of structural material is needed, for example for major dorsal augmentation, tip support, saddle-nose correction or revision surgery.[1][2][5]

For appearance, the graft is the scaffolding that lets a surgeon raise a low bridge, lengthen or project the tip, and straighten or rebuild a collapsed nose, producing a more defined profile and, in many patients, better balance with the rest of the face. Reviews describe costal cartilage as having large quantity and high biocompatibility, which is why surgeons turn to it when septal cartilage, the usual first source, is insufficient.[6][17]

In looksmaxxing discussion it appears as the structural-support option within hardmaxxing nose surgery, especially for people who want substantial projection or who have had earlier operations. Published evidence consists of surgical reviews and retrospective series, with grafts described both for Asian and African-descent rhinoplasty.[16][6][1] Because the harvest adds a second surgical site on the chest, the literature pairs descriptions of the aesthetic result with discussion of graft warping, resorption and donor-site pain.[1][6][7]

chain: Rib cartilage is harvested from the patient's own chest
It is carved into dorsal, tip or septal grafts
The grafts raise, lengthen or stabilise the nose, giving a more defined profile
angle.text: People who want a significantly higher bridge, a longer or more projected tip, or a rebuilt nose after previous surgery use rib cartilage because it provides more structural material than the septum or ear. The result is a firmer, more defined nose built from the patient's own tissue.

paras: Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article states that surgeons usually take cartilage from the septum first and use ear or rib cartilage when more is required, as often occurs in revision surgery.[3] The open approach makes it easier to secure grafts of skin, cartilage or bone, which the article notes is especially relevant in revision surgery and in thick-skinned noses.[3]

Costal cartilage is hyaline cartilage at the front ends of the ribs that extends the ribs forward and adds elasticity to the chest wall; it can be harvested for reparative use elsewhere, typically under general anaesthesia, with a small risk of pleural tear.[7] The cartilages tend to ossify superficially with age, most often in women aged 50 and over, which is one reason surgeons assess the donor cartilage before carving.[7]

Secondary or revision rhinoplasty, needed in roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasty operations according to Wikipedia, is technically more complicated because the support structures were deformed or removed earlier, and rib cartilage is one way to restore them.[3]

Reconstruction of the nose is among the oldest plastic procedures, with descriptions in the Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri and in the Sushruta Samhita, and modern endonasal rhinoplasty traced to John Orlando Roe's 1887 operation for a saddle nose.[3] Jacques Joseph described nose-reduction surgery through internal incisions in 1928, and the open approach introduced by Aurel Rethi in 1934 was promoted by Padovan, Goodman and Gunter from the 1970s onward; open exposure is what makes carving and fixing large grafts practical.[3]

Within that history, rib cartilage has been used when a patient's own septum cannot supply enough material. Reviews from the 2010s describe a shift in East Asian practice toward costal cartilage for dorsal and tip work, and refinements such as multilayered carving and 3D-printed carving guides aim to reduce warping and improve symmetry.[6][8]

Reviews of dorsal augmentation describe several ways of using costal cartilage. Solid block grafts and diced cartilage, with or without a wrapping material, are widely used for major dorsal augmentation; diced cartilage wrapped in temporal fascia is reported to resorb less and fit the dorsal contour, but is thought to have less predictable final height than block cartilage.[17][6] A 2021 overview of dorsal augmentation covers the basic concepts of cartilage grafting and emerging engineering approaches.[18]

A multilayered costal cartilage technique has been described to minimise warping and make carving easier, and 3D-printed implants and carving guides are discussed as ways to improve symmetry.[8] A 2023 review describes the subdorsal cantilever graft, a costal cartilage graft placed below the dorsum to raise the middle vault and caudal nasal bones for saddle-nose correction or the entire dorsum in ethnic augmentation rhinoplasty.[5]

For the tip, a 2015 paper describes a rib graft technique for anchoring an extended columellar strut, and a 2024 report describes a lollipop-like costal cartilage graft with a peach-shaped head for East Asian rhinoplasty.[2][10] Open rhinoplasty with costal cartilage, lateral crural tensioning and a septal extension graft, together with en bloc dorsal augmentation, is described as the workhorse approach in African-descendant rhinoplasty to improve tip definition and projection and augment the dorsum; the same review notes cartilage resections should be minimal and that oral isotretinoin and triamcinolone injection may improve tip definition.[16]

A retrospective cohort of 58 patients with osseocartilaginous dorsal onlay rib grafts (2000 to 2009) reported graft viability, mobility, warping, projection, airway function, revision and donor-site morbidity by telephone follow-up, and concluded the technique was stable and predictable for major dorsal reconstruction.[1]

A review of costal cartilage in Asian rhinoplasty says it has advantages over other grafting materials, namely large quantity and high biocompatibility, while also noting that it is technically demanding and associated with a high complication rate, including warping and infection, plus donor-site morbidity; several techniques have been proposed to reduce these problems.[6]

Wikipedia notes that swelling after any rhinoplasty can take a year or more to resolve fully, and that thick nasal skin can hide cartilage framework detail, which affects how definition from structural grafts shows through.[3]

Complications discussed in the literature include graft warping, infection, resorption, visibility or palpability of graft edges, the need for revision, and donor-site morbidity such as chest pain and pleural injury.[1][6][7] The chest harvest adds a second surgical site. Studies of related surgery have examined intercostal nerve block and continuous wound infiltration for pain control after rib harvest.[11][12]
General rhinoplasty risks listed by Wikipedia include swelling, visible scarring and unintended tissue damage, and smoking impairs healing through its effect on nasal blood supply.[3]

A retrospective cohort study of 58 patients who had osseocartilaginous rib grafts for dorsal augmentation between 2000 and 2009 assessed graft viability, warping, projection, airway function, revisions and donor site morbidity, concluding the technique was stable and predictable for major dorsal reconstruction.[1]

A randomised study of 44 patients undergoing Asian rhinoplasty with costal cartilage divided them into 3D-imaging and non-3D-imaging groups and surveyed the effect of the simulation.[13] A registered study examined allograft cartilage use in cosmetic and reconstructive rhinoplasty (n=50).[4]

Randomised and comparative trials in other surgery have tested the timing of intercostal block before or after rib harvest and wound infiltration versus nerve block after microtia reconstruction, addressing pain from rib cartilage harvest.[11][12]

Rib cartilage rhinoplasty is mentioned in hardmaxxing circles as the route to a large, structurally stable change in the nose, particularly for people seeking a higher radix or more tip projection or who have a weak septum. Discussion usually centres on choosing a surgeon experienced with costal cartilage, because reviews highlight that technique affects warping and complication rates.[6]

timeline.event: John Orlando Roe performs the first modern endonasal rhinoplasty, for a saddle nose.[3]
Aurel Rethi introduces the open approach that later makes large graft fixation practical.[3]
HNO review of nasal dorsal augmentation describes options including cartilage grafts.[15]
58-patient retrospective series on osseocartilaginous rib grafts published.[1]
Rib graft technique for anchoring an extended columellar strut described.[2]
Review of new trends in rib cartilage for Asian rhinoplasty.[6]
Review of subdorsal cantilever graft with costal cartilage.[5]
